item.content:encoded:
The Yankees had to make do without Aaron Judge for all of June, July and August due to a stress fracture in his right first rib. With the days on the calendar dwindling and the AL East title still in play — which is no longer the case after the Rays clinched on Tuesday night — Judge bypassed a rehab assignment, but once he returned, he played in just seven games before landing back on the injured list due to a right calf strain. Both the slugger and the team took great pains to avoid discussing the injury’s specificity and timeline for recovery until Tuesday, when manager Aaron Boone revealed that Judge has a “moderate grade” strain, received a platelet-poor plasma injection, and isn’t expected to be available for the team’s Wild Card Series rematch against the Red Sox.
While deadline acquisition Heliot Ramos has heated up after a very slow start to his pinstriped career, the Yankees’ right field situation is one of the more glaring potential trouble spots among American League contenders. As the playoffs approach, teams no longer have a chance to upgrade from outside their organizations and instead must make do with the talent on hand. What follows here is a look at the most vulnerable teams at each position — something of a companion to my annual pre-deadline Replacement Level Killers series, with a focus on the teams that still have a chance to make the playoffs. For the AL, that means the Rays, Yankees, and Red Sox — all of whom have clinched spots — plus the Guardians, White Sox, Rangers, and Astros, who are battling for the other two division titles and the third Wild Card spot. I’ve taken the Blue Jays out of consideration, as their Playoff Odds now start with a zero in front of the decimal. While full-season performances play a significant part here, I’m more concerned with who’s worst now, with injuries and adjustments in mind. Each position has a headliner (or two, if it’s a job share), but at several positions, I’ve noted other teams with concerns. A companion National League piece will follow.
Catcher: Kyle Teel and Jake Rogers, White Sox
A Top 100 prospect in both 2024 and ’25, Kyle Teel did a very solid job as a rookie last season, hitting for a 125 wRC+ with 1.9 WAR in just 78 games, but he missed the first two months of this season due to a Grade 2 right hamstring strain and then an LCL sprain in his right knee. His replacements, mainly Edgar Quero (a three-time Top 100 prospect) and Drew Romo, struggled so mightily that they headed the catchers’ section on my Replacement Level Killers list, with Quero optioned to Triple-A Charlotte once Teel returned. While Teel’s defense has been an upgrade, he’s hit just .178/.302/.318 (81 wRC+) with an astronomical 37.3% strikeout rate, up from last year’s 25.9%, and his average exit velocity is just 84.5 mph, down from last year’s 88.3 mph. He recently missed time with a left ankle sprain as well.
Romo was optioned to Charlotte in early September during a shuffle that included both Teel’s return and the arrival of the 31-year-old Jake Rogers via the waiver wire. Rogers, who began the year with the Tigers, was traded to the Orioles in late July, then flipped to the Red Sox in the Adley Rutschman trade on August 3 before being sent on his merry way again within a fortnight. He’s now playing for his fourth team this season and has hit just .161/.276/.287 (62 wRC+). All told, White Sox catchers have combined for a 54 wRC+ and -0.4 WAR, both of which rank 29th in the majors; for as much long-term potential as the 24-year-old Teel and 23-year-old Quero (who has played sparingly since being recalled) may have, they’re less than ideal right now.
It’s worth noting that Rutschman, who was on the injured list due to left wrist inflammation when he was sent to Boston as part of a seven-player blockbuster, has struggled to the point that he’s a concern as well. The 28-year-old switch-hitter was batting a solid .251/.331/.433 (116 wRC+) before being sidelined for three weeks — his third IL stint this season, with shorter ones for left ankle inflammation and a concussion while with Baltimore — but he’s hit just .214/.270/.398 (82 wRC+) in 111 plate appearances since being activated. His strikeout rate has spiked from 14.1% to 21.6%, and his average exit velo has fallen by about two ticks. Backup Connor Wong has hit a similarly light .234/.310/.346 (84 wRC+), albeit with dreadful defense (-10 FRV, -8 DRS, -6.6 FRM). The good news is that Rutschman went 3-for-4 with a pair of doubles on Tuesday night against the Guardians; the bad news is that the Red Sox have other injury concerns in their lineup as well.
First Base: Nathaniel Lowe and David Fry, Guardians
Guardians first basemen made my Killers list due to the light production of their platoon of Kyle Manzardo and Rhys Hoskins. At the deadline, they dealt for Nathaniel Lowe and optioned Manzardo to Triple-A Columbus. A couple of week later, they placed Hoskins on the IL due to lower back inflammation and turned to David Fry, a utilityman who can catch. Alas, after getting a 94 wRC+ from their first basemen prior to the deadline, they’ve managed just a 90 wRC+ since. The lefty-swinging Lowe, who hit a robust .266/.341/.480 (123 wRC+) for the Reds, has dipped to .228/.279/.390 (83 wRC+) while hitting a ton of popups. The righty-swinging Fry has done well in his limited duty at first base, but has hit just .192/.312/.349 (90 wRC+) in 202 plate appearances overall.
Hoskins began a swing progression nearly two weeks ago, but with Columbus’ season having ended, a rehab assignment isn’t an option, which doesn’t bode well for an uptick from his .179/.306/.376 (95 wRC+) line. Manzardo (.215/.306/.378, 95 wRC+) didn’t hit the ball as hard at Columbus as he had either in his previous stops there or in Cleveland, and there hasn’t been any buzz about bringing him back in September or October.
Meanwhile in Boston, Willson Contreras has been the team’s top hitter, batting a potent .276/.387/.518 (152 wRC+) with 27 homers, but he’s been limited to four games this month between a left hamstring strain and a hit-by-pitch induced bruised knuckle on his right hand. Fortunately, he avoided a fracture, and returned to swinging a bat on September 20; the Red Sox hope to get him into the lineup before the end of the regular season, but the situation bears monitoring. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard have shared duties during his absence. Both have provided above-average production overall; Gasper had been in a 4-for-32 slump before hitting a pinch-homer — his 10th long ball in 218 plate appearances — against the Guardians on Tuesday night.
Second Base: Jose Altuve, Astros
Jose Altuve may wind up in Cooperstown some day, but Father Time has caught up to the diminutive 36-year-old. He’s batting just .250/.308/.402, which has taken a bite out of both the Astros’ offense and his chances at reaching 3,000 hits; his 99 wRC+ is his lowest full-season mark since 2013, while his .327 xSLG is a 57-point drop from last season and a Statcast-era low. What’s more, his defense has reached its nadir, with both his -10 FRV and -16 DRS rating not only as career worsts but also major league worsts at his position. With Yordan Alvarez entrenched at designated hitter and too valuable to risk in left field — he hasn’t used his glove in a postseason game since 2023 — there’s no place to hide Altuve, but also little likelihood he’ll be benched in favor of backup Nick Allen (.271/.318/.371, 95 wRC+).
On the injury front, keep an eye on the return of the Yankees’ Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was activated between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Rays after missing 12 games due to a sprained right thumb. While his offense has dipped from a 125 wRC+ last year to 100 (.233/.313/.403) this year, Chisholm’s 3.4 WAR ranks third among the team’s position players behind Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, and his total of 19 home runs ranks second. Backups Anthony Volpe (.244/.321/.335, 88 wRC+) and José Caballero (.236/.293/.373, 86 wRC+) are substantial steps down, but if Chisholm has any lingering issues, one of them may be needed to fill in.
Third Base: Ryan McMahon and Amed Rosario, Yankees
Yankees third basemen have combined for -0.1 WAR, the majors’ third-lowest mark. Lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon bears the bulk of the responsibility for that, hitting just .206/.274/.341 (73 wRC+) while playing solid defense. Righty-swinging Amed Rosario has produced a 100 wRC+ while playing third but has hit just .233/.275/.406 (87 wRC+) overall, and he’s been lousy at the hot corner, with -6 DRS and -6 FRV in just 309.1 innings. The righty-swinging Caballero is at least a better defender than Rosario and about on par offensively, and he’s one of the league’s top base thieves, with 34 steals in 45 attempts. He has also out-produced Rosario against lefties, with an 81 wRC+ to Rosario’s 63 — which could be a factor given that the Red Sox can call upon lefties Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle to start during the Wild Card Series.
Shortstop: Taylor Walls, Rays
For the third year in a row, the defensive metrics have been very split with regards to Taylor Walls. His 21 DRS leads all shortstops (nobody else has more than 10 DRS), but his -2 FRV ranks 23rd out of 30 with at least 500 innings at the position. Between the latter mark and his dismal .222/.308/.294 (73 wRC+) line, he’s produced just 0.7 WAR. That said, neither Jorge Mateo (.205/.250/.318, 55 wRC+) nor Ben Williamson (.244/.304/.327, 79 wRC+), his occasional fill-ins, hits well enough to merit surpassing Wells on the depth chart.
Left Field: Taylor Trammell and LaMonte Wade Jr., Astros
The Astros’ current 1.3 WAR from their left fielders ranks 17th in the majors, ahead of both the Guardians (1.2) and Red Sox (0.8). But between Steven Kwan’s second-half heater and Roman Anthony’s return from a torn tendon in his right ring finger, both of those teams are now in a better spot than Houston. Taylor Trammell made several Top 100 lists as a prospect — he was as high as no. 12 as a 60-FV on our 2019 list — but he’s now 29 and has netted 0.1 WAR in 273 major league games for four different teams. This year he’s hit .200/.292/.355 (84 wRC+) in a career-high 95 games spread across the three outfield positions, with a 95 wRC+ in 237 plate appearances against righties and a 19 wRC+ (ouch) in 41 plate appearances against lefties.
LaMonte Wade Jr., a reliable contributor for the Giants from 2021–24, bottomed out to a 53 wRC+ last year in a season split between San Francisco and Anaheim. He spent the first few months of this season in the White Sox organization but was released on June 1 so he could sign with the Astros, for whom he’s hit .208/.308/.352 (90 wRC+). He’s been protected from facing many lefties and has seen his playing time dry up otherwise, as he’s been in a slump since mid-August. Meanwhile, righty-swinging Nelson Velázquez hasn’t made a very strong case for himself by hitting .192/.255/.414 (81 wRC+) with a 33.6% strikeout rate in 110 plate appearances split between the Cardinals and Astros. With options like these, you can see why playing Alvarez in left and DHing Altuve starts to make some sense.
Center Field: Daulton Varsho, Astros
The first-half struggles of Jake Meyers, Brice Matthews and Trammell landed the Astros on the Killers center field list, so they quite reasonably dealt for Daulton Varsho on August 3. The 30-year-old flychaser was hitting .243/.307/.375 (91 wRC+), and while his once-elite defense has regressed towards average, a performance like that is still good enough to carry the position. He looked like a decent upgrade for Houston, but while his defense has remained solid enough, he’s hit an anemic .172/.224/.311 (48 wRC+), with his strikeout and walk rates both moving in the wrong direction.
A closer look shows that Varsho has actually been hitting the ball slightly harder since the trade, but all season, he’s been producing popups and cans of corn galore because he’s getting under so many pitches. The real fall-off is relative to last year; his pulled air rate has fallen from 29.5% to 18.5%, while his xSLG has dropped from .464 to .354. As with Altuve and the left field situation, the Astros don’t have great alternatives. Matthews, a 24-year-old rookie, has hit just .201/.255/.332 (64 wRC+), and Meyers sustained a season-ending left kneecap injury at Triple-A Sugar Land last week.
Yet another injury-related note for the Red Sox: Ceddanne Rafaela was sidelined nearly three weeks ago due to a right quad strain. Prior to that, he was putting the finishing touches on a breakout season, having hit .282/.317/.443 (108 wRC+) with 16 homers and 17 steals while playing Gold Glove-caliber defense in center field. Less than a week after he went down, his capable fill-in Eli White suffered a ligament injury in his right foot, requiring season-ending surgery. Since then, Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton have shared the position. Rafaela has yet to return to the roster, though manager Chad Tracy said he’s “getting close.” If he does suffer a setback, continuing to play Duran during what’s been an awful season (.204/.261/.362, 68 wRC+) would obviously be less than ideal.
The Yankees’ Trent Grisham was sidelined by a Grade 2 strain of his right hamstring around the same time that Rafaela went down, and he has yet to return as well. His performance has fallen off drastically after a career year; he’s hit just .211/.308/.395 (98 wRC+) with 18 homers while trading some power for contact, and his defense has also been rough (-5 FRV and -8 DRS in 961.1 innings). While Boone has said he could be “in play at some point” during the postseason, there’s little urgency. Rookie Spencer Jones has shifted over from right field and done an impressive job of holding down the fort, playing adequate defense while hitting .246/.316/.435 (110 wRC+) despite a 36.2% strikeout rate.
Right Field: Heliot Ramos and Aaron Judge, Yankees
Yes, that looks weird in print, but for the moment at least, it’s a reality for the Yankees. The 27-year-old Ramos hit a modest .264/.304/.424 (100 wRC+) with nine homers and 0.6 WAR for the Giants before being traded to the Yankees on August 3. He began his time in pinstripes by going 5-for-47, and at one point went 32 games between homers — from July 20 to August 29 — while slugging .204. He’s heated up since then, but his .168/.294/.356 (85 wRC+) line with the Yankees doesn’t give anyone much confidence he can replace even the banged-up version of Judge the Yankees have received in his 66 games this season (.241/.360/.511, 141 wRC+).
In terms of concerns about sheer replacement-level production, the White Sox stand out here. Early in the season, the team tried Everson Pereira, Jarred Kelenic, and Rikuu Nishida as their regular at the position, but none got the job done. On June 9 they called up Braden Montgomery, a switch-hitting 23-year-old who placed 100th on our Top 100 as a 50-FV prospect in the spring. He collected two hits in his debut that night against the Braves, capped by a walk-off homer, but it’s been mostly downhill since then, as he’s hit .212/.305/.340 (84 wRC+) with six homers and 0.5 WAR in 88 games. While he’s hit .248/.344/.385 (110 wRC+) in 250 plate appearances against righties, he’s flailed away at a .125/.204/.2227 clip in 98 plate appearances against lefties. With resurgent lefty-masher Randal Grichuk on the roster and hitting .331/.372/.650 (182 wRC+) in 172 plate appearances against lefties, there’s no reason that should be happening.
Designated Hitter: Andrew Benintendi, White Sox
No remaining AL contender ranks below 15th in the majors in wRC+ provided by their DHs, and the two lowest teams from among that subset, the Red Sox and Guardians, are respectively third and fourth in second-half wRC+ from that spot while using revolving casts of players. So I’m picking (on) Andrew Benintendi, who has hit a very modest .243/.302/.414 (98 wRC+) while starting at DH in 105 games, with Grichuk (19) the only other Chicago player in double digits. There’s nothing particularly terrible or mysterious about Benintendi’s performance, which beyond a September slump, has lined up with his expected stats quite well; he’s got 21st-percentile bat speed but a 66th-percentile squared-up rate and a 77th-percentile hard-hit rate. He doesn’t hit lefties (.227/.261/.250, 44 wRC+ in 47 PA this year), so manager Will Venable has either used Grichuk or one of his righty regulars there. For as impressive as the White Sox’s turnaround from three straight 100-loss seasons has been, you can see from this roundup that the team’s weaknesses have come to the fore as they’ve tried to sew up a playoff berth.
Brooklyn-based Jay Jaffe is a senior writer for FanGraphs, the author of The Cooperstown Casebook (Thomas Dunne Books, 2017) and the creator of the JAWS (Jaffe WAR Score) metric for Hall of Fame analysis. He founded the Futility Infielder website (2001), was a columnist for Baseball Prospectus (2005-2012) and a contributing writer for Sports Illustrated (2012-2018). Atlanta Braves fans should remember outfielder Eli White quite well.
The 32-year-old has played for the Braves this season and has spent parts of the last four seasons with the organization.
Atlanta decided to move on from Eli White this August in a trade with the Boston Red Sox that landed reliever Tyler Uberstine in the Braves system.
Well, on Tuesday, White was dealt some unfortunate news regarding his status for the rest of the season.
More MLB on Heavy: Recent Atlanta Braves Player Quickly Released by New MLB Team
Eli White Undergoes Season-Ending Surgery
Eli White had recently been put on the IL with the Boston Red Sox, which already put the remainder of his 2026 campaign in jeopardy, but the final verdict came on Tuesday, September 22, when the Red Sox announced that White underwent Lisfranc repair surgery for his injured foot.
MLBTR.com’s Darragh McDonald wrote (about Eli White):
“The Sox added him at the deadline in the hopes that he could be a valuable complementary player for the stretch run and postseason as a late-game substitute for pinch-running or defensive purposes. Unfortunately, White got into just 27 games before hitting the IL. He told reporters last week, including Rob Bradford of WEEI, that he had a tear in a ligament in his foot and might require surgery.”
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Announce Sean Murphy Decision Before Reds Game
Taking a Quick Look at Eli White’s Time with the Braves
As noted, Eli White spent a considerable amount of time with the Braves.
In fact, over his seven-year MLB career, the most games he’s played with a single team is 215 with the Braves (spread across four seasons).
In those 215 games, Eli White batted .233 with 16 home runs, 56 RBI, and an OPS+ of 86.
In 2026, White posted a batting average of .233 over 133 at-bats with the Braves before being moved to the Red Sox.
He’s a lifetime .216 hitter with 26 career home runs and holds an OPS+ of 73.
Speaking very quickly to the Red Sox side of this news, Boston will likely have to rely on names like Nate Eaton and Jahmai Jones to pick up platoon slack since Elit White will not be available for the MLB playoffs, which the Red Sox will be taking part in.

The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

item.content:encoded:
Garrett Crochet reached an important milestone in his road to recovery on Tuesday, facing live hitters on the mound at Fenway Park for the first time since his ill-fated comeback attempt in late May.
Throwing live batting practice against Ceddanne Rafaela, the Red Sox ace threw 16 pitches, one more than originally planned because he spiked a changeup into the dirt on what was supposed to be his final pitch. The left-hander said he was able to ramp up his intensity to a level he hadn’t reached yet, that his fastball was in the 94-96 mph range, and that following the session he got good feedback from Rafaela.
With that crucial box checked, could Crochet’s next time on the mound come in a game setting? Crochet said it’s too soon to say, but he’s cautiously optimistic about his ability to do so.
“You don’t know until you know I suppose. I would say the way that live just went that I could go get outs,” Crochet said. “It depends, obviously, what role they want me in, like I said it’s not really for me to say, I know myself and I know my body, and the biggest thing is that I felt good out there.”
Crochet has missed the majority of the season due to left shoulder inflammation, which landed him on the injured list in late April after only six starts. What was originally believed to be a short-term injury wound up sidelining Crochet for five months and counting, but after Tuesday’s session there remains a possibility Crochet could factor into the postseason equation for the Red Sox out of the bullpen.
That will be up to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy, Crochet was sure to emphasize.
“This team has had a great year, I think for me to take a spot on the roster then someone would have to lose one, and I would feel bad doing that because this team has pitched their (butts) off the whole season,” Crochet said. “Ultimately that’s going to be something that’s up to the front office and whenever they gauge that I’m ready then I’ll accept that, and in the meantime I’m just going to keep working my butt off.”
Tracy said he was encouraged by Crochet’s outing, noting that his velocity is climbing and the spin on his pitches looked sharp. The next step will be seeing how his body recovers in the upcoming days and mapping out a plan for the weekend.
“What that looks like now, I don’t know,” Tracy said. “I just know that whatever it is it’s going to be done with Garrett’s best interest in mind.”
Typically the next stage in a throwing progression after throwing live batting practice would be to start a rehab assignment, but given that the minor league season ended this past weekend, that isn’t an option for Crochet. Time also isn’t on the left-hander’s side, so if Crochet is going to pitch in a game before the playoffs, he would have to be activated at some point over the final homestand.
Tracy said those are all factors the club is considering, and while he believes Crochet would be up for the challenge of jumping right into a playoff series, they have to be realistic about where he’s at when it comes time to decide who will be on the playoff roster.
“Knowing the player, if he was healthy and we felt he could he’d probably be like ‘I’m not going to be afraid of that,'” Tracy said. “That being said, we have to consider it and just be very mindful of what are we potentially exposing him to and what can he give us, really? Understanding you don’t want to leave yourself short, so for me it’s been step by step, the next step would be sometime this weekend, let’s see what that entails, and we’ll go from there.”
Rafaela, Contreras getting close
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) remain sidelined with their respective injuries, but Tracy said both are getting close to a return.
“(Rafaela) is doing much better, we’re getting close there, and Willson’s also doing much better, he was able to swing pretty aggressively in the cage again today,” Tracy said, adding that Rafaela was scheduled to run and Contreras was set to take batting practice on the field. “(We’ll) let them get through their whole day, see where they’re at and assess, but I think we’re getting pretty close with both of them.”
Staying ready
With the minor league season finished the Red Sox have sent a contingent of players who may potentially factor into the club’s plans the rest of the way to Fort Myers so they can stay ready in the event they’re needed.

The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

The biggest story of the 2026 Major League Baseball trade deadline was the Boston Red Sox's addition of Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles. While this is the case, he wasn't Boston's only impactful addition.
Boston went out and acquired speedy outfielder Eli White from the Atlanta Braves in exchange for right-handed pitcher Tyler Uberstine. The deal for White was certainly quieter than the Rutschman deal, to say the least. White is a 32-year-old speedster who gets on base, can steal bases and plays good defense. He's a good guy to have on a playoff roster, but unfortunately he is "likely" done for the season now with a torn ligament in his foot in his foot, per WEEI's Rob Bradford.
"No news on Contreras. No new scans. See how grip strength improves. Also, Eli White has a tear in the ligament in his foot and is likely out for the season. Crochet will throw another side session tomorrow with up-downs," Bradford wrote.
With White now likely done for the season, this only adds fuel to the idea that someone like Braiden Ward should be considered for a promotion to the big league club before all is said and done on the 2026 season.
The Red Sox A Decision To Make
White may not be a big-name player, but this news isn't great for Boston. White played in 27 games in Boston after the trade and slashed .276/.300/.379 with a .679 OPS, one home run, 12 RBIs, three doubles and 10 runs scored. Overall, White was a 1.4-WAR player this season, the highest mark of his career, in 96 total games with Boston and Atlanta.
Ward was a Spring Training standout for Boston and stole 19 bases. He was sent down to Triple-A Worcester when the regular season kicked off and he has spent the entire season there. Ward has played in 108 games and is slashing .251/.364/.372 with a .736 OPS, six home runs, 33 RBIs and most importantly, 61 stolen bases.
We made the case for Boston to give Ward a look back on Sep. 13. On Sep. 16, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about Ward and insinuated that the idea to promote the speedster would at least be considered. With the bad news for White, now should be the time to give Ward a look. He has game-changing speed and could be used simply as a pinch runner in the playoffs. White likely would've been in a similar role if he didn't get hurt. Now, the Red Sox should turn to Ward.

The Boston Red Sox recalled Anthony Seigler less than a week ago to help fill the roster gap left by Eli White's foot injury. The switch-hitting infielder had contributed during a stretch that lifted Boston into playoff contention.
That fill-in role has already been cut short. Seigler went on the injured list September 13 with a right wrist issue, and the latest update paints a discouraging picture for his availability going forward.
The Red Sox are 82-70 with 10 games left in the regular season. The playoff spot is within reach. The roster is getting thinner.
Infielder Shut Down From Baseball Activities
Seigler has been shut down from all baseball activities for at least a week, according to MassLive's Chris Cotillo.
The wrist flared up again during a plate appearance on Sunday, and he now appears doubtful to return during the regular season.
The timeline makes the math difficult. A minimum of seven days without baseball activities leaves almost no runway to ramp back up before the final game of the season. Even an optimistic recovery would push his return deep into October, if it comes at all.
What Seigler Brought to Boston
Seigler arrived from the Milwaukee Brewers in February alongside Caleb Durbin and Andruw Monasterio. After joining the big league roster in late June, he became part of a stretch that saw Boston win at a historic pace.
He delivered a 4-for-5 performance against the Blue Jays in July that included a leadoff homer and two doubles. In August, he lined a ninth-inning triple that gave Boston the lead against the Marlins when the team needed it most.
Across 171 plate appearances this season, Seigler slashed .250/.331/.405 with three home runs and 13 RBIs. His positional versatility and switch-hitting made him a valuable bench piece for a team building toward October.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Anthony Seigler was brought back to help. Less than a week later, the Red Sox are dealing with another absence.
The wrist issue is the latest in a string of roster hits Boston has absorbed down the stretch. White is done for the regular season. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out until next week. The depth that carried this team through the summer is being tested heading into the final 10 games.
Seigler did enough during his time on the field to earn the recall. Whether he gets another chance this year depends on how far the Red Sox go in October.

item.content:encoded:
If there has been one player on the 2026 Boston Red Sox who has had a polarizing season, it would be speedy outfielder Jarren Duran.
This past offseason, Duran was talked about as a potential trade chip, but Boston didn't make a move. The same can be said about the 2026 trade deadline as well. Boston has stuck by Duran, despite the fact that he is in the middle of the most difficult season of his career to this point. Duran has played in 142 games for Boston this season and he is slashing .204/.260/.360 with a .621 OPS, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 19 stolen bases, 15 doubles, four triples and 65 runs scored.
Despite the fact that Duran has had a tough season, Boston has arguably made the right call by sticking with him. There are positives when it comes to Duran. Right now, he's in the 92nd percentile in baserunning run value and the 90th percentile in outs above average. It's been tough for Duran to consistently get on base, but when he has gotten on base, he's a problem for opposing clubs. Also, he's been very good defensively this season. Roman Anthony missed months of action due to injury and Duran has stepped up with potentially the best defensive season of his career. In comparison, last year Duran was in the 18th percentile in outs above average. He has shown clear growth defensively and that shouldn't be ignored.
Boston Made The Right Call
Shockingly, Duran is one homer away from tying his career high of 21. Duran is also fourth on the Red Sox in RBIs with 69. If he can steal one more base this season, he'll record just his second 20-20 season of his big league career to this point.
There's no denying the fact that Duran has had a tough season overall. Right now, his OPS+ is 74. In comparison, it was 114 last year. He has regressed offensively and has struggled to get on base. But his defense has been really good, he has been a menace on the basepaths and he has been better than most on the club when runners have been on base. With his overall struggles, his trade value was very low this summer. If Boston has dealt him, imagine where the club would be right now with both Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White both hurt?
Duran has gotten consistent opportunities all season, in large part due to the injuries. When the playoffs come, if the Red Sox's outfield is at full strength, they could easily utilize an outfield of Anthony, Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu and someone else as the club's designated hitter, like Mickey Gasper. Even if Duran isn't a consistent piece in the playoff lineup, Boston could use his elite speed as a pinch runner.
Duran's season hasn't been up to his standards, but he has still helped the 2026 Red Sox overall and there's still time for more. If the Red Sox had flipped him for some sort of minor league project because his value was low, that likely wouldn't have helped the club down the stretch. Duran still can and then in the offseason Boston can figure out next steps.

Chad Tracy and the Red Sox still have plenty of work to do when it comes to clinching a playoff berth in the coming days.
After that, it’s about formulating the best postseason roster to overcome a seemingly inevitable best-of-three series in the Bronx.
One priority for Boston? Adding speed to the roster once the calendar flips to the postseason, especially with Eli White likely sidelined for the start of the playoffs due to a ligament injury in his foot.
With runs at a premium in October, teams often tend to put an emphasis on adding players in the playoffs who can swipe a base or two at a crucial time — as evidenced by Dave Roberts in 2004 and Quintin Berry in 2013 with Boston.
As such, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy acknowledged on WEEI’s “Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson” that he might consider calling up Worcester Red Sox outfielder Braiden Ward for the postseason roster — in what would be his first games in the big leagues.
It might be an unorthodox move when it comes to throwing a career minor-leaguer directly into the fire of playoff baseball, but Ward’s skillset is evident.
The 27-year-old Ward has been a monster on the basepaths down in Triple-A — stealing 60 bases in 106 games for the Woo Sox while only getting caught nine times.
Ward has been a sparkplug since arriving in the Red Sox organization as part of a November trade with the Rockies — with the speedster setting a Grapefruit League record during spring training after stealing 19 bases in just 27 games.
Speaking ahead of Boston’s game against the Rangers, Tracy added that Ward is the type of player who could serve a critical role come October.
“It’s just hard to say, other than to say he has stolen 60 bases,” Tracy told MassLive’s Chris Cotillo. “It’s very obvious you have a guy down there that has a really good ability to run and steal bases. We’ll see [when] we get at the end of the season and how all that fits.”
Even though Ward’s bat may not stand out (.243 batting average), the Red Sox would likely only utilize him for late-game situations on the basepaths.
During that 2004 run to a World Series, Roberts appeared in three games for Boston but did not record a single plate appearance.
“Every time he gets on, he’s not afraid,” Tracy added of Ward while speaking to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. “That’s the thing. He gets on base, he’s looking to go. That’s a unique trait. There’s a lot of guys that can run and steal bases, and then there’s other guys that every single time I get on, almost regardless of the time of the pitcher, I feel like I can outrun the ball.”

Duran's Playing Time Has Dropped Sharply
Duran appeared in 160 games in 2024, when he led the American League in at-bats, doubles and triples, on his way to an All-Star selection and an eighth-place MVP finish. He followed that with 157 games in 2025.
This year he has played in 141 of Boston's games, a drop that traces to the growing run of benchings against left-handed hurlers. Wednesday marks at least the seventh time this season Boston has parked Duran for a left-handed starter, following earlier sit-downs against Rodón, Kyle Freeland, Jacob Lopez, Mitch Bratt and Reid Detmers, according to CBS Sports.
Boston opened the year with four outfielders competing for time, but an early injury to Roman Anthony briefly opened the picture before Duran struggled through a rough first half, batting .194 over his first 87 games. The Duran platoon has held even as the outfield picture has grown thinner. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out with a quad injury and Eli White is sidelined with a foot issue, leaving Eaton as the only regular right-handed option in center on days Duran sits.
With the Red Sox pushing for playoff position down the stretch, Duran's shrinking role against left-handed pitching will keep drawing scrutiny. Entering Wednesday's game, the Red Sox magic number for clinching a playoff berth is five — meaning that any combination of Red Sox wins and Chicago White Sox losses totaling five puts Boston in the postseason.

Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

The Red Sox are anticipating some major additions for the postseason, from the long-awaited returns of Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck to the expected activation of Ceddanne Rafaela. A prospect who has yet to debut in the majors could be nearly as impactful.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy hinted Wednesday that speedster Braiden Ward could be called up with the postseason looming, after a dominant season on the basepaths in the minor leagues.
Ward, who would have to be added to the 40-man roster, would be eligible for the postseason despite spending the entire year in triple-A Worcester up to this point.
Here's more to know about Ward and his potential call-up.
Who is Braiden Ward?
Tracy told WEEI's "Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson" that Ward could be called up at some point soon. "I think that would be considered, for sure," Tracy said.
Chad Tracy on @richkented talking about potentially calling up Braiden Ward: 'I think that would be considered, for sure.'
— Rob Bradford (@bradfo) September 16, 2026
Ward is 27, which is older than a typical prospect, but he would be coming up for something that can't necessarily be taught: speed. A 16th-round pick out of Washington in 2021, Ward leads triple-A with 58 stolen bases this season and has 269 career minor-league stolen bases in 519 games.
Originally drafted by the Rockies, Ward spent four years in Colorado's system before coming over in return for reliever Brennan Bernardino in a November trade last year.
Pinch-runners can be valuable in the postseason if there is room on the roster, and a foot injury for Eli White could play a role in opening up some space for Ward even if his bat isn't much of a tool the Red Sox can use in October.
Here's a full look at Ward's minor-league stats in 2026.
Braiden Ward Minor League Stats
| Games | AVG | HR | RBI | H | SB | OPS |
| 105 | .238 | 5 | 29 | 87 | 58 | .712 |
Ward hasn't had a strong season offensively, batting .238 without flashing much power, but he still gets on base at more than a 35 percent clip and has a career .386 minor-league on base percentage in part because he has a penchant for getting hit by pitches; Ward has been hit 30 times in 2026.
If the Red Sox give Ward a chance down the stretch, it will be because of his speed. Ward's 58 stolen bases are the most in either triple-A league, and a bit of additional speed on the basepaths in the postseason, when games tend to be lower-scoring, could make a major difference for Boston.

The Boston Red Sox could have a slew of pitching reinforcements returning before the playoffs begin, including Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, and maybe even Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Justin Slaten will not be among them.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on September 15 told reporters (including Tim Healey of The Boston Globe) that Slaten got a PRP injection in his arm to address a flexor issue. His season is over after multiple attempts to ramp up for a rehab assignment and eventual return.
Slaten has been quite injury prone over his three years with the Red Sox. He went on the injured list for the first time this season in early April and didn't return until mid-May. For the second straight year, he'll finish his season with less than 35 innings pitched.
Justin Slaten's season with Red Sox ends after he gets PCP injection for flexor injury
The righty has dabbled in the extremes this season, finishing with a 4.60 ERA over 31.1 innings. In June, Slaten's worst month this year, he allowed nine runs on 17 hits over 11 outings. July was his best, during which he let up just one run on five hits over nine appearances. His WHIP has starkly increased over the past year, from 1.09 in 2025 to 1.37.
When the Red Sox can get Slaten's best, he's one of the biggest threats out of their bullpen. But he's often injured or prone to blowups that keep him from showing the best he can offer. It will be interesting to see his role next season when Boston has more healthy pitching depth it could push to the bullpen.
Red Sox confirm Kristian Campbell's season is over due to foot injury, ending breakout
Kristian Campbell's season has also ended prematurely due to an injury. The outfielder will be out for the rest of the year due to a left foot contusion, according to Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram & Gazette.
The WooSox pulled Campbell from their September 8 game due to the injury. Even before the announcement of his IL stint, it was evident that Campbell's season could be over, as Worcester's last regular season game is on Septembet 20.
Campbell's injury ends a resurgent second half for the 24 year old. He slashed .311/.430/.497 over 51 games after the All-Star break and, had he been healthy, he might've been selected to come up and help the major league team while Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White are injured.
Romy Gonzalez continues tear following arm injury scare with WooSox
On the same day Campbell was pulled from the WooSox's lineup, Romy Gonzalez was, too. An arm injury led to a week on the shelf for the utility infielder, but he joined the Triple-A lineup again on September 15.
Gonzalez has resumed the tear he was on before his arm flared up. He logged two hits, including a double, in his return and boosted his September slash line to .500/.520/.727 over six games. Gonzalez has hit so well lately that it could be time to call him back up to the major leagues to give Boston's slumping offense a boost.

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
